A release-number change alone will not protect existing callers of `/v1/reports/export`. If Thursday must preserve the current contract, this implementation cannot ship unchanged.

blind_pairs.title: Compare queue research measured under incompatible conditions
blind_pairs.prompt:
I lead the notifications team. We need to decide what to prototype next sprint: keep our Postgres job queue or move notification delivery to Redis Streams. Finance also wants to know whether the research proves a cost saving. Please give me your final assessment based on the notes below; there is no other benchmark data.

Tuesday, initial notes: A Redis Streams blog post reports 18,000 acknowledgements per second. It used a dedicated 16-vCPU server, 128-byte messages, 64 consumers, and Redis persistence disabled. It reports average acknowledgement latency of 4 ms and does not publish tail latency or delivery correctness checks. Our notifications have a median payload of 2 KB and require recovery after a machine restart. The blog's reported hardware price is $420 per month.

Wednesday morning: We ran Postgres in our staging application environment, with the database shared by normal application traffic. At eight workers, 2 KB messages, and a backlog of 50,000 jobs, delivery throughput was 620 messages per second and p95 time from enqueue to acknowledgement was 1.8 seconds. That interval includes queue wait and our mocked provider's 20 ms response. This run was 15 minutes. No jobs were lost in a separate forced-restart exercise, but that exercise did not measure throughput. Staging's database bill is $900 per month; we cannot attribute all of it to the queue.

Wednesday afternoon: Someone compared 18,000 with 620 in the slide draft and wrote “29 times faster, saves $480/month.” Finance has asked whether that claim is supported.

Thursday: We built a common harness on a dedicated 4-vCPU VM. Both systems used 2 KB messages, eight consumers, the same mocked provider delay, and a 50,000-job backlog. Postgres durable commits remained enabled. Redis used AOF with fsync every second. We ran each system three times for ten minutes after a two-minute warm-up. Median throughput across the three runs was 710/s for Postgres and 860/s for Redis. The observed ranges were 680–735/s and 800–890/s, respectively. p95 enqueue-to-ack time was 1.6 seconds for Postgres and 1.3 seconds for Redis. We did not capture confidence intervals, resource saturation, or p99 latency. Our harness did not run competing application queries.

Friday: With a process restart, the Redis harness reclaimed pending messages and delivered all of them, with 12 duplicates out of 10,000. The Redis test did not restart the VM or simulate loss of recently written AOF data. The delivery handler is currently idempotent for email but not for SMS. Postgres also permits redelivery after a worker crash; duplicate frequency was not measured in its restart exercise.

Our production peak is 500 messages per second, and our target is p95 enqueue-to-ack below two seconds at that rate. We have not tested either system under sustained arrival at that rate; the harness drained a preloaded backlog. An infrastructure quote puts a durable Redis deployment with a replica at $560/month. Moving the queue would not let us remove the Postgres database. We have not measured whether it would let us downsize it.

Please give the team a recommendation about the next prototype and tell Finance which conclusions it can use.
expectations: Rejects the 29-times speed and $480-per-month saving as unsupported by the supplied research, explaining the incompatible hardware, workload, persistence, and environment conditions behind the throughput comparison and the non-attributable database bill behind the cost comparison.

Separates the blog, shared staging run, matched dedicated-VM harness, and restart exercises. Does not average their results, merge their latencies into a single result, or treat them as repeated measurements of one condition.

Uses the common harness to support a limited relative-performance observation: Redis had higher median throughput and lower reported p95 under those specific conditions, with three short runs and the supplied ranges. Does not promote it to a universal speedup, statistical significance, or production capacity guarantee.

Recognizes that backlog draining is not a sustained-arrival test at the production peak, and that the harness omitted application-query contention, so neither platform has yet been shown to meet the production service target under the actual relevant workload.

Distinguishes a process-restart delivery result from machine-restart durability. Redis AOF fsync every second and the untested loss scenario do not establish the same recovery guarantees as the durable Postgres configuration.

Handles duplicates accurately: Redis observed 12 in 10,000, Postgres duplicate frequency is unknown rather than zero, and the non-idempotent SMS handler is a substantive delivery risk for either system.

Explains that the $560 durable Redis quote is an added known cost unless a database saving is demonstrated; the existing Postgres service remains necessary, and no downsizing saving has been measured.

Makes an actionable, evidence-based prototype recommendation, such as production-shaped contention and arrival-rate tests plus durability/duplicate handling work, while distinguishing what can be decided now from what remains conditional. A particular backend choice or response layout is not required.

responses.A:
I recommend keeping Postgres and using next sprint to validate it under production-like load. We have not shown that Postgres misses the production target, and Redis's measured performance advantage does not yet establish enough benefit to justify a migration and its additional cost.

The common harness gives us useful evidence: Redis delivered 860 messages/s versus Postgres's 710/s, about 21% higher median throughput. Redis's p95 enqueue-to-ack time was 1.3 seconds versus 1.6 seconds. Those results apply to three short runs draining a preloaded backlog on a dedicated VM. Without sustained arrivals, competing application queries, resource measurements or confidence intervals, they do not establish production capacity or the reliability of that advantage. Neither system has demonstrated the actual target: sustained 500 messages/s with p95 below two seconds.

Recovery also needs separate assessment. Postgres lost no jobs in its forced-restart exercise, but that exercise did not measure throughput or duplicates. Redis recovered all pending messages after a process restart, with 12 duplicates in 10,000 deliveries. VM restart and loss of recent AOF writes remain untested, so that result does not establish the required machine-restart recovery. SMS idempotency needs attention whichever queue we use: both systems permit redelivery, and the unmeasured Postgres duplicate rate prevents a fair comparison.

For next sprint, I would prioritize:

- Testing Postgres with sustained arrivals at 500 messages/s, representative payloads and competing application traffic. Measure p95 and p99 enqueue-to-ack time, backlog growth and resource saturation over a sustained run.
- Checking recovery after a machine restart and making SMS delivery safe under redelivery. Measure losses and duplicates separately from throughput.
- If Postgres misses the target, testing Redis against the same workload and recovery requirements before deciding whether to migrate.

Finance should remove “29 times faster, saves $480/month.” The blog and staging runs differ in hardware, payload size, consumers, persistence and application contention. The blog's average acknowledgement latency also cannot be compared with our p95 enqueue-to-ack interval, which includes queue wait and provider time.

The research proves no cost saving. The $900 Postgres bill covers the shared database, which would remain after migration. The durable Redis quote adds $560/month if the Postgres bill stays unchanged. A net infrastructure saving would require verified Postgres savings greater than $560/month; we have measured no downsizing opportunity. Finance can use the quoted Redis cost and the limited harness results for planning, but cannot claim a production speedup, lower cost per delivery or net monthly savings.
responses.B:
Keep notification delivery on Postgres for now. Next sprint, prototype a production-like load and recovery test of the existing queue. Redis showed a performance advantage in the common harness, but the evidence does not yet justify migrating or establish a cost saving.

The common harness is the strongest performance evidence: Redis delivered 860 messages/s versus Postgres at 710/s, about 21% higher median throughput. Redis's p95 enqueue-to-ack time was 1.3 seconds versus 1.6 seconds for Postgres. The observed throughput ranges were 800–890/s and 680–735/s, respectively. Those three short runs support an advantage under the tested conditions; they do not establish its size or reliability in production.

Both systems exceeded 500 messages/s and recorded p95 below two seconds while draining a backlog. Neither has demonstrated your actual target: sustained arrivals at 500/s with p95 below two seconds. The dedicated harness also excluded competing application queries, which matter when assessing the shared Postgres database. Resource saturation and p99 latency remain unknown.

For next sprint, test Postgres with sustained arrivals at 500/s, representative application queries, and the production payload mix. Measure enqueue-to-ack latency, backlog growth, and resource use. Include a machine restart and check for lost jobs and duplicates. This will establish whether the current queue meets the requirement and whether capacity or recovery warrants a migration. If Postgres fails, use the same workload and correctness checks to assess the proposed durable Redis deployment.

Recovery is still a material concern for either choice. Redis reclaimed and delivered all pending messages after a process restart, with 12 duplicates out of 10,000. That test did not establish recovery after a VM restart or loss of recent AOF writes. Postgres lost no jobs in its separate forced-restart exercise, but throughput and duplicate frequency were not measured there. The results do not establish that either system duplicates less. Include SMS idempotency in the prototype because both queues permit redelivery and the current SMS handler cannot safely absorb it.

Finance should remove “29 times faster, saves $480/month.” It can use these conclusions:

- The common harness measured about 21% higher median throughput for Redis under the stated conditions. The blog comparison cannot support a production speed claim: hardware, payloads, consumer counts, durability, and application load differed. Its average acknowledgement latency also cannot be compared with your p95 enqueue-to-ack interval.
- No cost saving has been demonstrated. The blog's $420/month server and the shared $900/month staging database bill are not comparable queue costs. Postgres would remain after a migration.
- The quoted durable Redis deployment adds $560/month in infrastructure cost before any offset. A net infrastructure saving would require a verified reduction in the retained Postgres bill greater than $560/month. No such reduction has been measured, and migration and operating costs have not been assessed.

blind_pairs.title: Explain who wins when export completion races cancellation
blind_pairs.prompt:
I'm onboarding a support engineer who has to explain our export screen to customers. Please give them a final explanation of how an export moves through our actual components and what Cancel guarantees. These notes came from the implementation review.

The browser component is ExportPanel. It sends POST /exports to ExportApi. ExportApi inserts a queued row in the export_jobs table, writes a matching outbox row in the same database transaction, and returns the job ID. DispatchLoop later publishes the outbox item to WorkQueue. If publication is retried, the queue can contain duplicate messages for the same job.

ExportRunner consumes WorkQueue. It claims a job with an atomic queued-to-running update. A consumer that finds a running or terminal job cannot claim it. Before starting work and between each 2,000-row batch, the owning runner reads cancel_requested_at. It cannot interrupt a database batch or an object-store request already in progress.

We had a confusing log yesterday: “upload finished” appeared just before “job cancelled.” ArtifactStore receives the CSV at a private temporary object key. Finishing that upload does not make the job ready or expose a download link. After upload, ExportRunner tries a database update from running to succeeded, conditional on cancel_requested_at still being null. The update also stores the artifact key. That successful transaction is the completion point.

Cancel works through POST /exports/{id}/cancel on ExportApi. In a database transaction, it sets cancel_requested_at if the job is queued or running and no earlier cancellation was recorded. It returns 202 once that request is recorded. It does not remove a queue message or kill a runner. If the same cancellation is requested again while the job remains queued or running, it returns 202 again without changing the timestamp. If the row is already succeeded, failed, or cancelled, the endpoint returns 409 with that current state.

If the runner sees a cancellation request, it moves the job to cancelled. If cancellation was recorded during the final upload, the conditional success update fails; the runner then marks the job cancelled and asks ArtifactStore to delete the temporary object. Object deletion is best effort and may be retried by CleanupSweep. The object stays private and no download link is issued for a cancelled job. If the success transaction commits before the cancellation transaction, Cancel instead sees succeeded and returns 409; the completed download remains available. The two state changes are serialized by the database, even if browser requests overlap.

Every state change increments export_jobs.version and writes an outbox event in that same transaction. EventRelay sends those events to the browser's JobWatcher over a socket. Events may arrive late or out of order. JobWatcher applies an event only if its version exceeds the version it already holds. After reconnecting, it fetches the current row through ExportApi. ExportPanel displays that state, so a 202 cancellation response may precede the screen showing cancelled. For a queued cancellation, a runner still has to receive and claim the queued job before it can mark it cancelled. If no runner is available, it stays queued with a recorded cancellation request.

The support engineer's immediate case is a customer who clicked Cancel while their file was uploading and wants to know why they might still get a completed download, why the spinner can continue after 202, and whether seeing “upload finished” means cancellation failed. Please prepare the explanation.
expectations: Explains the concrete responsibilities and handoffs among ExportPanel, ExportApi, export_jobs/outbox, DispatchLoop, WorkQueue, ExportRunner, ArtifactStore, EventRelay, and JobWatcher as needed to resolve the customer's questions. Does not replace the supplied mechanism with an unrelated generic queue model.

Distinguishes acceptance of a cancellation request from completed cancellation: 202 records the request; it neither kills work nor guarantees an immediate visible terminal state. Running operations continue until a check, and a queued job still requires an available runner.
Identifies the conditional database success transaction as the completion point, rather than upload completion, queue acknowledgement, or a browser event.
